title: Coping strategies (compensatory and adaptive)
description: Enduring coping patterns a client uses across situations. Group compensatory holds strategies developed to cope with core beliefs and conditional assumptions, as in the coping strategies box of the cognitive conceptualization diagram. Group adaptive holds flexible, helpful coping that a formulation names as strengths or treatment goals. Situation-level acts are in bh.
sources: Beck-etal-2015 § Ch. 2 Theory of Personality Disorders

concepts.label: Avoiding negative emotion
concepts.definition: Habitually avoiding, suppressing or numbing unpleasant emotions, and situations that might trigger them, to protect against feared vulnerability.
concepts.client_wording: Doing whatever it takes not to feel upset, sad or scared.
concepts.example: Never talking about feelings and keeping constantly busy after a loss.

concepts.label: Perfectionistic striving
concepts.definition: Persistently pursuing very high standards and judging self-worth by meeting them, despite costs, to avoid failure or criticism.
concepts.client_wording: Pushing yourself to be perfect, because anything less feels like failing.
concepts.example: Spending every weekend polishing reports that already meet the brief.

concepts.label: Overpreparation
concepts.definition: Preparing far beyond what a task requires, to prevent failure, exposure of inadequacy or uncertainty.
concepts.client_wording: Preparing much more than needed so nothing can possibly go wrong.
concepts.example: Scripting every word of a five-minute team update.

concepts.label: Overresponsibility
concepts.definition: Taking excessive responsibility for others' wellbeing and for preventing harm, beyond one's real role or control.
concepts.client_wording: Feeling it is your job to keep everyone safe and everything on track.
concepts.example: Checking on adult siblings daily and fixing their problems for them.

concepts.label: Avoiding intimacy
concepts.definition: Keeping relationships distant, limiting self-disclosure or ending closeness, to avoid rejection, hurt or exposure.
concepts.client_wording: Keeping people at arm's length so they cannot get close enough to hurt you.
concepts.example: Ending relationships once they become serious.

concepts.label: Seeking recognition
concepts.definition: Pursuing achievement, status or admiration to prove worth and offset an underlying sense of inadequacy.
concepts.client_wording: Needing to achieve and be admired to feel good enough.
concepts.example: Taking on every high-profile project to be seen as the best.

concepts.label: Attention seeking
concepts.definition: Drawing others' attention through dramatic, emotional or entertaining displays, to secure care, approval or connection.
concepts.client_wording: Needing to be noticed and finding ways to make people pay attention to you.
concepts.example: Escalating stories of crises when friends seem distracted.

concepts.label: Avoiding confrontation
concepts.definition: Habitually avoiding disagreement, criticism or conflict, even when important issues need raising.
concepts.client_wording: Keeping the peace at any cost and never raising problems with people.
concepts.example: Never telling a partner about an ongoing hurt, to avoid an argument.

concepts.label: Overcontrol
concepts.definition: Trying to control situations, people and outcomes tightly, leaving little room for others' input, uncertainty or spontaneity.
concepts.client_wording: Needing to be in charge of everything so nothing goes wrong.
concepts.example: Redoing a partner's chores because they were not done "properly".

concepts.label: Dependence on others
concepts.definition: Relying on others to decide, protect or do tasks, and presenting as helpless, to cope with feeling incapable or alone.
concepts.client_wording: Leaning on others to decide or do things because you feel you cannot manage alone.
concepts.example: Asking a parent to call the bank and make every decision.

concepts.label: Pleasing others
concepts.definition: A lasting pattern of putting others' wishes first and seeking their approval, to avoid rejection or disapproval.
concepts.client_wording: Always trying to keep people happy with you, even at your own expense.
concepts.example: Shaping career, clothes and opinions around what others might want.

concepts.label: Excessive self-reliance
concepts.definition: Refusing or avoiding help and insisting on handling everything alone, to avoid appearing weak, incompetent or indebted.
concepts.client_wording: Never asking for help, because needing help feels like weakness or failure.
concepts.example: Struggling for weeks with a task rather than asking a colleague.

concepts.label: Hypervigilance to others
concepts.definition: Watching others closely for signs of hostility, rejection or deception, and staying guarded and slow to trust.
concepts.client_wording: Always watching people for signs they might hurt, reject or trick you.
concepts.example: Rereading a friend's messages for hidden criticism.
sources: Beck-etal-2015 § Ch. 12 Paranoid, Schizotypal, and Schizoid Personality Disorders
Beck-etal-2015 § Ch. 2 Theory of Personality Disorders

concepts.label: Self-sacrifice
concepts.definition: Routinely meeting others' needs at the expense of one's own, to avoid guilt or causing others pain.
concepts.client_wording: Always putting other people's needs before your own, even when it costs you.
concepts.example: Caring for relatives every evening while one's own health suffers.

concepts.label: Avoiding challenges
concepts.definition: Steering away from new tasks, goals or opportunities where failure or inadequacy might be exposed.
concepts.client_wording: Not trying new or hard things in case you fail.
concepts.example: Not applying for a promotion despite encouragement.

concepts.label: Asserting superiority
concepts.definition: Acting superior, entitled, dominant or critical of others, to ward off underlying feelings of inferiority or vulnerability.
concepts.client_wording: Putting others down or acting above them so you never feel small.
concepts.example: Belittling colleagues' ideas in meetings.

concepts.label: Rigid rule-following
concepts.definition: Relying on strict rules, routines, lists and order to manage uncertainty and avoid mistakes.
concepts.client_wording: Sticking tightly to rules and routines, and feeling uneasy when things change.
concepts.example: Refusing any change to a weekly schedule, even for a celebration.
sources: Beck-etal-2015 § Ch. 2 Theory of Personality Disorders

concepts.label: Concealing vulnerability
concepts.definition: Hiding perceived flaws, needs or true feelings behind a competent or cheerful front, to avoid rejection or judgment.
concepts.client_wording: Hiding your real self or struggles behind a front so no one sees weakness.
concepts.example: Always appearing upbeat at work while privately struggling.

concepts.label: Problem solving
concepts.definition: Defining a problem, generating options, weighing them, choosing and trying one, then reviewing the result.
concepts.client_wording: Breaking a problem into steps and working through options to sort it out.
concepts.example: Listing three ways to handle rent arrears, then calling the landlord.

concepts.label: Seeking emotional support
concepts.definition: Turning to trusted people for comfort, understanding or a chance to talk feelings through.
concepts.client_wording: Talking to someone you trust about how you feel.
concepts.example: Calling a friend after a hard day to talk it through.

concepts.label: Seeking practical help
concepts.definition: Asking others for advice, information or practical assistance with a problem.
concepts.client_wording: Asking people for advice or hands-on help when you need it.
concepts.example: Asking a colleague to show how to use new software.

concepts.label: Self-soothing
concepts.definition: Using comforting sensory or caring actions, such as warmth, music or gentle touch, to calm distress kindly.
concepts.client_wording: Doing gentle, comforting things for yourself when you are upset.
concepts.example: Taking a warm bath with calming music after a panic attack.

concepts.label: Acceptance
concepts.definition: Allowing unwanted thoughts, feelings and unchangeable realities to be present without struggle, while still choosing helpful action.
concepts.client_wording: Letting feelings or facts be there without fighting them, so you can move forward.
concepts.example: Making room for grief while still going to work.

concepts.label: Balanced thinking
concepts.definition: Deliberately weighing the evidence and generating a more balanced or helpful view of a situation.
concepts.client_wording: Stepping back to look at the whole picture and find a fairer way to see things.
concepts.example: "One mistake does not cancel years of good work."
sources: Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 9 Alternative or Balanced Thinking

concepts.label: Self-compassion
concepts.definition: Responding to one's own suffering or mistakes with warmth, understanding and encouragement rather than criticism.
concepts.client_wording: Treating yourself with the kindness you would show a good friend.
concepts.example: "Anyone would struggle with this; I am doing my best."

concepts.label: Mindful awareness
concepts.definition: Noticing thoughts, feelings and sensations in the present moment as passing events, without judging or acting on them.
concepts.client_wording: Noticing thoughts and feelings as they come and go without getting caught up in them.
concepts.example: Noticing "I am having the thought that I will fail" and returning to the task.

concepts.label: Calming the body
concepts.definition: Using slow breathing, muscle relaxation or similar methods to lower physical arousal, used flexibly rather than as a safety behavior.
concepts.client_wording: Using slow breathing or relaxing your muscles to settle your body.
concepts.example: Doing slow breathing for five minutes before a hard conversation.
sources: Thwaites-Freeston-2005 § Safety behaviors versus adaptive coping

concepts.label: Planned distraction
concepts.definition: Briefly and deliberately shifting attention to absorbing activities to get through acute distress, then returning to the problem.
concepts.client_wording: Doing something absorbing for a while to get through a hard moment.
concepts.example: Doing a puzzle for 20 minutes until an urge to drink passes.

concepts.label: Physical activity
concepts.definition: Using exercise or movement in moderation to lift mood, reduce tension and support sleep.
concepts.client_wording: Moving your body, like walking or dancing, to help your mood and stress.
concepts.example: Walking for 20 minutes at lunch on low days.
sources: Martell-etal-2022 § Ch. 5 Activity Scheduling and Structuring

concepts.label: Values-based action
concepts.definition: Choosing and taking actions guided by personal values, even when mood or motivation is low.
concepts.client_wording: Doing things that matter to you, even when you do not feel like it.
concepts.example: Attending a child's school event despite low energy.
sources: Martell-etal-2022 § Ch. 6 Avoidance Modification, Solving Problems, and Value-Directed Behavior

concepts.label: Assertive communication
concepts.definition: Clearly and respectfully stating needs, opinions, requests or refusals while considering the other person.
concepts.client_wording: Saying what you need, or saying no, clearly and kindly.
concepts.example: "I cannot take this on this week, but I can help next Monday."

concepts.label: Opposite action
concepts.definition: Acting opposite to an emotion's action urge when the emotion does not fit the facts or acting on it would not help.
concepts.client_wording: Doing the opposite of what a feeling urges, when acting on it would not help.
concepts.example: Calling a friend when sadness urges hiding at home.

concepts.label: Urge surfing
concepts.definition: Observing a craving or urge rise, peak and fall like a wave, without acting on it.
concepts.client_wording: Riding out an urge like a wave until it passes, without giving in.
concepts.example: Noticing the urge to binge, rating it, and watching it fade over 20 minutes.

concepts.label: Expressive writing
concepts.definition: Putting thoughts and feelings about stressful events into words, in writing or speech, to make sense of them.
concepts.client_wording: Writing or talking about what happened and how you feel, to make sense of it.
concepts.example: Writing for 15 minutes about a difficult week.

concepts.label: Spiritual or religious coping
concepts.definition: Drawing on religious or spiritual beliefs, practices or community for comfort, meaning or guidance.
concepts.client_wording: Finding strength or comfort in your faith, prayer or spiritual practice.
concepts.example: Praying and attending services for support after a bereavement.
